INLA-style posterior approximation for any log-posterior

Source: R/inla-vanilla.R
inla_vanilla.Rd

Approximates the posterior of a parameter vector from its log density alone, using the approximation pipeline of INLAvaan (Jamil & Rue, 2026a, 2026b) with no latent field and nothing model-specific. The pipeline has four stages:

  1. Joint Gaussian (Laplace). The posterior mode \(\vartheta^*\) and the inverse Hessian \(\Omega\) there give a Gaussian approximation \(N(\vartheta^*, \Omega)\) and the Laplace estimate of the log marginal likelihood.

  2. VB mean correction. The Gaussian is recentred at \(\tilde\vartheta = \vartheta^* + \hat\delta\), the mean that maximises its expected log-posterior, with the covariance unchanged.

  3. Skew-normal marginals. For each parameter, the log-posterior is scanned along the conditional mode path of the Gaussian, corrected for the changing volume of the other parameters, and fitted by a skew-normal \(SN(\hat\xi_j, \hat\omega_j, \hat\alpha_j)\).

  4. Gaussian copula draws. sampling() couples the skew-normal marginals through the correlations of \(\Omega\).

Stages 2 and 3 are optional and independent of each other. vb = "off" skips the VB correction, which leaves the marginals unchanged (they are scanned around the mode) but gives the Laplace log marginal likelihood. marginals = "gaussian" skips the scans and uses the Gaussian's own marginals \(N(\tilde\vartheta_j, \Omega_{jj})\), centred at the VB mean (or at the mode when vb = "off"); sampling() then draws from the joint Gaussian. So vb = "off", marginals = "gaussian" is the Laplace approximation alone, and marginals = "gaussian" alone is the Laplace approximation with the VB correction.

Usage

inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init,
  grad = NULL,
  hess = NULL,
  ...,
  vb = c("onestep", "full", "off"),
  marginals = c("skewnormal", "gaussian"),
  width = c("trace", "cmp", "tk"),
  tk_fallback = FALSE,
  cores = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE,
  silent = FALSE,
  control = list()
)

Arguments

logpost

A function logpost(theta, ...) returning the log-posterior density (up to a constant) at the named numeric vector theta, on the unconstrained scale. See the section on writing logpost.

init

A named numeric vector of starting values. Its length sets the number of parameters and its names label them; unnamed values are called theta[1], theta[2], ..., and a repeated name is numbered in the same way.

grad

Optional function grad(theta, ...) returning the gradient of logpost as a numeric vector. When NULL (the default), finite differences are used.

hess

Optional function hess(theta, ...) returning the Hessian of logpost, the m x m matrix of its second derivatives (a sparse matrix from the Matrix package, and a number when m = 1, work too). It needs grad. When NULL (the default), finite differences of grad are used.

...

Further arguments passed to logpost, grad and hess, such as the data. As in stats::nlminb(), they come after the gradient and the Hessian, and the arguments after them (vb, marginals, width, tk_fallback, cores, verbose, silent, control) must be given by their full names, so data arguments cannot partially match them. A data argument cannot take one of those names. The arguments before them can be matched, as in nlminb(): a data argument named g or gr would be taken as grad, and one named h or he as hess, so give it a longer name.

vb

The VB mean correction: "onestep" (the default) takes one Newton step from the mode, "full" iterates to the VB solution, and "off" (or FALSE) leaves it out. TRUE means the default, and abbreviations such as "one" work too. See the section on the VB correction. The correction enters the log marginal likelihood, and the skew-normal means are checked against it (see summary.inla_vanilla()).

marginals

The marginal of each parameter: "skewnormal" (the default) fits a skew-normal to a scan of the log-posterior; "gaussian" uses the Gaussian marginal of the Laplace approximation, centred at the VB mean unless vb = "off", with no scans. Abbreviations such as "skew" and "gauss" work too.

width

How each skew-normal scan accounts for the changing volume of the other parameters, the width term \(\gamma_j(t) = -\frac12 \log|H_{-j}|\) (see the section on the width term). With m parameters and n_grid scan points, per parameter:

  • "trace" (the default): its linear term \(\gamma_j' t\), as in INLAvaan, from 4 grad calls, and one more for all the parameters together (2m + 5 logpost calls without grad), on top of the n_grid - 1 logpost calls of the scan.

  • "cmp": the exact width term along the same straight scan, from the Hessian of the other parameters at each scan point: about n_grid - 1 times 2(m - 1) grad calls (n_grid - 1 hess calls with hess, or n_grid - 1 times (m - 1)m logpost calls without grad).

  • "tk": the Laplace marginal of Tierney and Kadane (1986). At each scan point the other parameters are moved to their conditional mode by stats::nlminb(), started from the straight scan, and the height and the width term are taken there: the calls of "cmp" plus those of n_grid - 1 conditional optimisations, typically 5 to 20 logpost and grad calls each with grad, and many more without.

With one parameter the three are the same. Abbreviations work. Ignored for Gaussian marginals.

tk_fallback

Logical. Rescan with width = "tk" every parameter whose ridge_bend is flagged (above 0.25, see summary.inla_vanilla())? Default FALSE, so that a fit costs what width says and gives the same marginals whatever its diagnostics. The parameters rescanned are listed in fit$fallback and by summary.inla_vanilla(). Ignored for Gaussian marginals and with width = "tk".

cores

The number of CPU cores for the skew-normal scans, and for loo() and waic() on this fit. NULL, the default, follows future::plan(), and is serial if no plan is set. 1 is serial whatever the plan. Needs the future package (see the section on parallel computation).

verbose

Logical. Print a full diagnostic of each stage under its progress line? Default FALSE. See the section on output.

silent

Logical. Print nothing at all, and muffle the warnings and messages raised during the fit? Default FALSE. The warnings are still recorded in fit$warnings. Cannot be combined with verbose = TRUE.

control

A list of tuning parameters; see the section on control.

Value

An object of class inla_vanilla, with methods for print(), summary(), coef(), plot(), sampling(), diagnostics() and timing(). It is a list holding, among other things:

  • summary: the posterior summary table (mean, SD, quantiles, mode).

  • mode, cov: the Laplace mode and covariance.

  • mean_vb: the VB-corrected mean (the mode when vb = "off").

  • sn: the skew-normal parameters xi, omega and alpha per parameter (with alpha = 0 for Gaussian marginals).

  • vb, marginals, width, tk_fallback, cores, verbose, silent: the settings the fit used (width is NA for Gaussian marginals).

  • fallback: the parameters that tk_fallback rescanned with width = "tk" (empty when there were none).

  • logml: the log marginal likelihood, and logml_laplace its Laplace part.

  • diagnostics: the checks of each stage, which diagnostics() returns under INLAvaan's names and summary.inla_vanilla() explains. optim holds the return code, message and iterations of stats::nlminb(), the gradient of minus the log-posterior at the mode (grad), the whitened gradient there (grad_mode), and the condition number of the Hessian in posterior-SD units (hess_cond). vb holds the iterations of the VB correction, whether it stopped at the first step (one_pass), whether it fell back to stats::nlminb() (fallback), and the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the shift (kld_global); it is NULL when vb = "off". marginals is a data frame with a row per parameter: mode_shift_sigma, kld, vb_shift, vb_shift_sigma, nmad, alpha, unscanned_mass, vb_step_sigma, grad_gap, mean_gap, gamma1, tails and ridge_bend, with NA for the checks the fit did not run, and width, the width method of each scan (see the section on the width term).

  • scan: the scans the skew-normals were fitted to, for plot(fit, type = "sn_fit"): the grid z in posterior SDs from the mode, the log-posterior at each point (logpost, a column per parameter: along the CMP, or at the conditional modes for width = "tk"), the width term added to it (width, zero at the mode), and the log scale factor logC of each fit on that grid. It is NULL for Gaussian marginals.

  • workers: the number of parallel jobs the scans ran on, 1 for a serial fit (see the section on parallel computation).

  • timing: the elapsed time of each stage of the fit, in seconds, which timing() returns.

  • warnings: the messages of the warnings raised during the fit, as a character vector of plain text, each message once (empty when there were none). They are recorded whether or not silent is TRUE.

Writing logpost

The approximation works on an unconstrained scale: every parameter must be free to take any real value. Reparameterise anything constrained, for example a standard deviation \(\sigma > 0\) as \(\log\sigma\), a probability as its logit, or a correlation as its Fisher \(z\). Means and regression coefficients need no change.

Return -Inf wherever the density is zero or cannot be evaluated, such as outside the support or where a matrix is not positive definite (NA and NaN count the same). The scans and the VB nodes reach several posterior SDs from the mode, and an error raised there stops the fit.

logpost is then the log density of the parameters you pass. When a prior is stated on the natural scale, include the log-Jacobian of the transformation: with \(\vartheta = \log\sigma\) and a prior \(p(\sigma)\), the prior term is \(\log p(e^\vartheta) + \vartheta\). Leaving it out targets a different posterior, not a worse approximation of the same one, and nothing downstream can detect it.

The choice of parameterisation also sets the quality of the approximation, since each parameter gets its own skew-normal on the scale you choose. Scales on which the posterior is close to Gaussian (log standard deviations, Fisher-\(z\) correlations, logits) work best. Natural-scale or derived quantities are available through sampling(fit, fun = ...).

The log marginal likelihood is an estimate of \(\log p(y)\) only when logpost returns the full \(\log p(y, \vartheta)\), including every normalising constant of the likelihood and the prior. Otherwise it is off by the missing constants.

Accuracy

The skew-normal marginals capture skewness that the Laplace approximation misses, and they are accurate to the extent that a skew-normal fits each marginal (see the diagnostics in summary.inla_vanilla()). Like INLAvaan, each marginal is scanned along a straight line through the mode, and the changing volume of the other parameters enters only to first order. When a parameter's spread depends strongly on another, poorly determined parameter, its marginal comes out too narrow, by a factor that vanishes as O(1/n). Examples are a regression coefficient or a mean when the noise SD is uncertain. For a normal mean with unknown variance the SD is about 11% too small at n = 12, 3% at n = 50, and under 1% at n = 200. The ridge_bend diagnostic of summary.inla_vanilla() flags this narrowing where it predicts about 10% or more. By default (width = "trace") this is the scan of INLAvaan; width = "tk", or tk_fallback = TRUE for the flagged parameters only, removes the narrowing at a higher cost (see the section on the width term).

A skew-normal also cannot follow a tail heavier than a Gaussian's. In a structural equation model with 39 parameters and n = 75, the data could not keep two residual variances away from zero, so on the log scale their posteriors had a long, exponential left tail, set by the prior. Checked against MCMC, those two skew-normal marginals were less than half as wide as the posterior, with the 2.5% quantile about 2 posterior SDs too high; the other 37 were within 7% in SD. On the variance scale, where the tail near zero is compressed, the two were much closer: means 0.2 posterior SDs too high and SDs 10 to 15% too small. INLAvaan's marginals of this model are the same as inlavanilla's: Jamil and Rue (2026a, Section 4.4) find the same miss in the lower tail of a variance near zero, the boundary pile-up that a unimodal skew-normal cannot capture. No check is aimed at this. The ridge_bend diagnostic of summary.inla_vanilla() flagged one of the two (0.44), but the other's ridge bend (0.11) was no larger than that of marginals within 7% in SD, and the tails check, which looks only 4 posterior SDs either side of the mode (the Laplace SDs), missed both.

The width term

Each skew-normal scan follows the conditional mode path (CMP) of the Laplace Gaussian, \(\vartheta(t) = \vartheta^* + t v_j\) with \(v_j = \Omega_{\cdot j} / \sqrt{\Omega_{jj}}\), so that \(t\) counts posterior SDs. The log marginal is then about the height of the log-posterior along the path plus the width term \(\gamma_j(t) = -\frac12 \log|H_{-j}(t)|\), where \(H_{-j}\) is the negative Hessian of the log-posterior with row and column j deleted: the log-volume of the other parameters. width sets how it is taken, in three levels that each remove one error:

  • "trace", the default and INLAvaan's, linearises it, \(\gamma_j(t) \approx \gamma_j' t\), with the slope from whitened differences of the gradient (Jamil & Rue, 2026a, Corollary 3.3).

  • "cmp" takes \(\gamma_j(t)\) exactly along the same path. Its difference from "trace" is the error of the linearisation.

  • "tk" moves the other parameters to their conditional mode at each point of the scan and takes the height and the width term there: the Laplace approximation of the marginal (Tierney & Kadane, 1986), INLA's "Laplace strategy". Its difference from "cmp" is the error of the straight path, which the ridge_bend diagnostic of summary.inla_vanilla() predicts.

The skew-normal is fitted to the corrected heights in the same way for all three, on the same grid. tk_fallback = TRUE keeps the cheap scan for every parameter but those whose ridge bend is flagged, and rescans those with "tk". In fit$diagnostics$marginals, width gives the method each parameter used and gamma1 the slope of its width term at the mode (for "cmp" and "tk", a central difference across the mode). The ridge bend of a parameter scanned with "tk" is still reported, but not flagged.

Gradients and Hessians

grad is optional. Without it, derivatives come from finite differences of logpost, and the number of calls grows with the square of the number of parameters m. The mode and Hessian take about m^2 + 6m calls, and the marginals about m(n_grid + 2m + 6), with 2(m - 1) more for each parameter whose ridge bend is above 0.1. The VB correction takes (m + 1)(m + 2) calls, or that many per sweep with vb = "full": it needs no derivatives, because Stein's identity gives the expected gradient from values of logpost alone. With vb = "full", the VB mean is then exact when the log-posterior is a polynomial of degree four in whitened coordinates, and up to degree six with grad. On test models it was about 0.01 posterior SDs from exact VB (0.003 with grad), and up to 0.1 on a strongly skewed posterior (0.03 with grad), against a VB error of 0.01 to 0.2 SDs from the posterior mean itself. On the most skewed posteriors the VB correction may then not settle, and the fit says it has not converged (see summary.inla_vanilla()); grad is the remedy.

With grad, every stage is more accurate. The fit is also faster when a gradient call costs about as much as a logpost call, as a hand-written gradient usually does, since it then makes far fewer calls in all. A gradient by automatic differentiation (RTMB, TMB) costs about two, and beyond a handful of parameters the fit is still several times faster than without one (four times at m = 39). The default VB correction, vb = "onestep", takes 2m + 1 gradient calls, about as many as one numerical Hessian, and vb = "full" takes at most (m + 1)(m + 2) + 1 per sweep, usually about four sweeps. Beyond a handful of parameters the marginals are the slowest stage, along with the VB correction under vb = "full". vb = "off" skips the VB correction (and its term in the log marginal likelihood), and the skew-normal marginals do not depend on it; marginals = "gaussian" saves the calls of the scans.

hess is optional too, and needs grad, as in stats::nlminb(). With it, stats::nlminb() takes Newton steps to the mode, and the Hessian at the mode is the supplied one. The VB correction does not use it, nor do the default marginals, whose volume correction takes 4m + 1 grad calls for all the parameters together, where a Hessian each would cost far more. width = "cmp" and width = "tk" do use it. The fit is the one grad alone gives, to the error of its finite differences (about 1e-8, relative), except that the mode is found more precisely. A dense Hessian costs about m gradients, so this takes a little longer: a structural equation model with 39 parameters and an automatic-differentiation Hessian (RTMB) took 0.18 s with it and 0.17 s without.

The fit goes straight to the mode: at init it only checks that logpost, grad and hess return finite values of the right shape. A supplied grad is compared with logpost at the mode, from differences the fit takes there anyway, so at no cost in calls, and its Jacobian there is checked for symmetry, with a warning if either check fails (see grad_gap in summary.inla_vanilla()). A supplied hess is checked at the mode against central differences of grad, along two directions, with a warning if it does not match; grad is then not compared with logpost, since no differences of logpost are taken. Any R function works for logpost, grad and hess, including compiled code (Rcpp, TMB) and RTMB, which differentiates R code. An RTMB function can return the log-posterior itself, and its obj$fn, obj$gr and obj$he are then passed as they are. For a TMB template that returns the negative log-posterior, pass function(x) -obj$fn(x), function(x) -as.vector(obj$gr(x)) and function(x) -obj$he(x), with init = obj$par; its repeated names (one per element of a parameter vector) are numbered, as beta[1], beta[2], and so on. TMB gives no Hessian for a model with random effects.

The VB correction

The VB mean correction moves the centre of the Laplace Gaussian towards the posterior, keeping its covariance. It maximises the expected log-posterior under that Gaussian, so that at the solution the gradient, averaged over the Gaussian, is zero.

vb = "onestep" takes the first Newton step towards that solution, with the Laplace curvature, and stops. With a gradient, the average is taken over the mode and \(\pm\sqrt 3\) posterior SDs along each principal axis of the covariance. Without one, it is one pass of Stein's identity on the rule of vb = "full". Most of the movement is in that step, and exact VB is itself an approximation to the posterior mean with an error of the same order. If the first step is over 2.5 posterior SDs, or a node fails, the iteration carries on with capped steps, within the number of calls that the mode and Hessian took. diagnostics() then has vb_step_sigma, the step still to go, which is NA after a single step. After a single step the fit checks that it delivered what it promised: vb_gain_ratio in diagnostics() is the rise in the expected log-posterior over the rise the step assumed, and a ratio below 0.5 raises a warning. A large first step can also overstate the VB term of the log marginal likelihood, so after a shift above 1 posterior SD, which is flagged, compare models with care: vb = "full" may be closer.

vb = "full" iterates to the solution, on a degree-5 rule with at most (m + 1)(m + 2) + 1 nodes, and hands over to stats::nlminb() if it does not converge.

Parallel computation

Set cores to run the per-parameter scans of the skew-normal marginals in parallel:

cores <- future::availableCores(omit = 1)
fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init, width = "tk", cores = cores)

availableCores() counts the cores the machine offers, and omit = 1 leaves one free. A fit never asks for more workers than the machine offers. The results and the progress line are those of a serial fit. A long scan uses all the cores, a shorter one fewer, and a scan expected to take under a second stays serial. The mode, the Hessian and the VB correction stay serial, so the gain is largest with width = "tk" or "cmp", where the scans are nearly the whole fit: about 7.5 times faster on 12 cores on test models. With the default width the scans are about half of a slow fit, and it was about 1.5 times at most.

cores needs the future package, which is optional. It uses forked workers where those are safe, in a terminal on macOS or Linux, and separate R sessions elsewhere: on Windows, in RStudio, and in Positron's console, which refuses to fork. Forks share everything. Separate sessions need the package installed, not just loaded with devtools::load_all(), and are sent your functions and data. Compiled code (Rcpp, TMB, RTMB) cannot be sent, so the fit first checks that a worker gets the same value at the mode, and otherwise runs serially with a message.

To use separate sessions with compiled code, rebuild it on each worker: put whatever creates it in a function, and call that function again when the process is not the one that started the fit. With RTMB and random effects (without them, RTMB needs none of this):

build <- function() {
  RTMB::MakeADFun(model, parameters, random = "u", silent = TRUE)
}
obj <- build()
pid <- Sys.getpid()
rebuild <- function() {
  if (Sys.getpid() != pid) {
    obj <<- build()
    pid <<- Sys.getpid()
  }
}
logpost <- function(theta) {
  rebuild()
  -obj$fn(theta)
}
grad <- function(theta) {
  rebuild()
  -obj$gr(theta)
}

With Rcpp, rebuild() calls Rcpp::sourceCpp(file, cacheDir = dir) instead, with a dir of your own so that the workers share one compiled copy. The RTMB and Rcpp articles on the package website have worked versions.

With cores left at NULL the fit follows a plan set with future::plan(), and runs serially if there is none, so a plan can apply to every fit in a session. cores = 1 runs serially whatever the plan. loo() and waic() use the setting of the fit.

Control

control is a list with any of:

  • n_grid: number of grid points per skew-normal scan, spread over \(\pm 4\) posterior SDs (default 21).

  • log_threshold: grid points whose log-posterior falls more than this below the maximum are ignored in the skew-normal fit (default -6).

  • vb_maxit, vb_tol: iteration limit (default 25) and convergence tolerance in posterior SDs (default 1e-3) for the VB correction's fixed-point iteration, with vb = "full" and when a one-step correction has to iterate. A step over 1.5 posterior SDs is cut to 1.5. With vb = "full", if two steps in a row are cut, or it has not converged after vb_maxit steps, stats::nlminb() takes over.

  • nlminb: a list of stats::nlminb() controls for the mode search. iter.max and eval.max both default to 5000, and trace = 1 prints its iterations.

Output

By default each stage prints one line as it finishes, with the time it took, and shows a progress bar while it runs for longer than half a second, or than the option cli.progress_show_after when it is set. In knitr or Quarto documents, where a bar cannot redraw in place, a larger cli.progress_show_after in the setup chunk keeps bars out of the output. Warnings, such as a gradient that does not match logpost, are signalled as usual. A fit whose checks look off, such as a mode that was not reached, ends with one warning that lists them, as INLAvaan's does (see summary.inla_vanilla() and diagnostics()).

verbose = TRUE adds a full diagnostic of the fit, in grey lines under each stage. It reports what the fit computes anyway, with no further calls of logpost or grad:

  • Before the mode search: the parameters, where the derivatives come from, and logpost at init.

  • The mode: the message, iterations and evaluations of stats::nlminb(), and whether it was restarted with the parameters rescaled; the log-posterior at the mode, the whitened gradient there (which decides the restart) and the largest Newton step in posterior SDs (which the fit-time warning checks); how the Hessian was taken (and, for a supplied grad, the asymmetry of its Jacobian and its gap from logpost, or, for a supplied hess, how far it is from central differences of grad); the largest posterior correlation and the smallest eigenvalue of the correlation matrix, which is near zero when some combination of the parameters is poorly identified, and the condition number of the Hessian in posterior-SD units; and the Laplace log marginal likelihood.

  • The VB correction: the largest step, in posterior SDs, at each fixed-point iteration, whether Anderson acceleration or the fallback optimiser was used (and, after the fallback, the step still to go where it landed, and whether it was rerun from there), the largest shift, and the term it adds to the log marginal likelihood.

  • The marginals: the shape, NMAD, ridge bend, tails, unscanned mass and volume correction gamma1 of each parameter, with the values that summary.inla_vanilla() flags marked.

  • The calls of logpost, grad and hess in each stage, and in all, with the total time.

For the iteration trace of stats::nlminb() itself, pass control = list(nlminb = list(trace = 1)).

silent = TRUE prints nothing, for simulations and other repeated fits: no progress bars and no stage lines, and every warning and message raised during the fit, including those of logpost, grad and hess, is muffled. Errors are still raised. Output printed with cat() or print(), by logpost, grad, hess or the trace of stats::nlminb(), is not captured.

Whatever the level, the warnings raised during the fit are recorded in fit$warnings, so that a simulation can check them afterwards.

References

Jamil, H., & Rue, H. (2026a). Approximate Bayesian inference for structural equation models using integrated nested Laplace approximations (arXiv:2603.25690 [stat.ME]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.25690

Jamil, H., & Rue, H. (2026b). Implementation and workflows for INLA-based approximate Bayesian structural equation modelling (arXiv:2604.00671 [stat.CO]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2604.00671

Tierney, L., & Kadane, J. B. (1986). Accurate approximations for posterior moments and marginal densities. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 81(393), 82–86. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1986.10478240

See also

sampling() for posterior draws and derived quantities, summary.inla_vanilla() and diagnostics() for diagnostics.

Examples

# Normal data with unknown mean and standard deviation, on the scale
# (mu, log sigma)
set.seed(1)
y <- rnorm(30, mean = 5, sd = 2)

logpost <- function(theta, y) {
  mu <- theta[["mu"]]
  sigma <- exp(theta[["log_sigma"]])
  sum(dnorm(y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, 10, log = TRUE) + # prior on mu
    dexp(sigma, rate = 1, log = TRUE) + # prior on sigma ...
    theta[["log_sigma"]] # ... and its Jacobian
}

fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0), y = y)
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 10 iterations [2ms]
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.25σ [1ms]
#> ✔ Fitted 2 skew-normal marginals [6ms]
fit
#> ── INLAvanilla ──────────────────────────────── Skew-normal + one-step VB ──
#> 
#> Log marginal likelihood: -66.38 · Converged in 10 iterations (14ms)
#> 
#>               Mean     SD   2.5%    50%  97.5%   Mode
#> 1 mu         5.159  0.327  4.517  5.159  5.800  5.159
#> 2 log_sigma  0.616  0.129  0.377  0.610  0.885  0.599

# The posterior of sigma itself, through the draws
sigma <- sampling(fit, fun = function(theta) exp(theta[["log_sigma"]]))
quantile(sigma, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#>     2.5%      50%    97.5% 
#> 1.444354 1.832695 2.455869 

# A full diagnostic of each stage
fit <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0),
  y = y,
  verbose = TRUE
)
#> ℹ 2 parameters: mu and log_sigma
#>   Derivatives by finite differences of logpost
#>   logpost at init -481.47
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 10 iterations [1ms]
#>   nlminb: relative convergence (4), after 10 iterations (14 function and 26
#>     gradient evaluations)
#>   logpost at the mode -65.06, whitened gradient 8.8e-08σ, Newton step
#>     8.8e-08σ (warning > 0.1σ)
#>   Hessian by second differences of logpost: 6 calls, and 12 more to set the
#>     steps
#>   Posterior correlation matrix: largest correlation -0.0042 (mu,
#>     log_sigma), smallest eigenvalue 1
#>   Hessian condition number 1, in SD units (warning > 1e+08)
#>   Laplace log marginal likelihood -66.41
#>   63 logpost calls
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.25σ [1ms]
#>   Fixed-point steps, largest over the parameters (σ): 0.25
#>   One step, accepted (guard > 2.5σ)
#>   Gain ratio 0.95 (warning < 0.5)
#>   Largest shift 0.25σ, for log_sigma (warning > 1σ)
#>   KL term 0.031, giving a log marginal likelihood of -66.38
#>   16 logpost calls
